Puente medieval de piedra sobre el río L: A medieval stone bridge over the River Lune, with three ribbed arches. Legend says the devil built it in exchange for the first soul to cross, and an old woman threw a bun to the other side so her dog crossed first. Since 1932 cars have used the bridge next to it, the Stanley Bridge: this one is for walking, riding or cycling.
Mirador detrás de la iglesia de St Mary,: A viewpoint behind St Mary's church, above a bend in the Lune. Turner painted it, and in 1875 the writer John Ruskin called it «one of the loveliest scenes in England, therefore in the world». There is a bench to sit and look.
La plaza del mercado del pueblo, con su: The town's market place, with its stone cross. Kirkby Lonsdale has held a market on Thursdays since 1227, when the king granted it a charter.
La iglesia de Kirkby Lonsdale. Las parte: The church of Kirkby Lonsdale. The oldest parts are Norman, from the 12th century, with very thick columns carved with diamonds. Ruskin's View is behind it.
La iglesia de Casterton, junto al colegi: Casterton's church, next to the school, built between 1831 and 1833.
Casa victoriana de 1848 que diseñó el ar: A Victorian house from 1848 designed by the architect Ewan Christian (of the National Portrait Gallery in London) for the Reverend David Barclay-Bevan. Today it is rented as a whole for holidays and weddings, like a hotel, and you can go inside here: the ground floor has rooms of our own design (gold drawing room, dining room, billiard room with a bar, conservatory, kitchen and more). By the entrance to the estate, on the west side of the A683, there is an old protected stone milestone.
Círculo de unas 20 piedras pequeñas de l: A circle of about 20 small Bronze Age stones, about 18 m across, high on the hillside. You can see the whole valley from here.

Es Casterton, en el valle del río Lune (: This is Casterton, in the valley of the River Lune (Cumbria, in the north of England): Casterton, Sedbergh Prep school, the Casterton Golf Club next to it, Kirkby Lonsdale with the Devil's Bridge, and 3 km of meadows, dry-stone walls and hedges around them. Everything comes from real data: the terrain and the height of every tree, wall and roof from the Environment Agency LIDAR; the houses and paths from OpenStreetMap and the Ordnance Survey; the colour of the ground from the Sentinel-2 satellite. You start in a small plane: jump, glide and land wherever you like. Real golf, the school inside, the horses, the drone and the sports were added in later stages.

`

Casterton is a small village in Cumbria, in the valley of the River Lune, 2 km from Kirkby Lonsdale. To the east rise the Casterton and Barbon fells; to the north, the Howgill Fells; to the west, the Lake District.

What's here

  • Casterton, Sedbergh Prep: Sedbergh School's prep school for children up to 13, in the old Casterton School (founded in 1823), with its chapel, boarding houses, sports fields, swimming pool and stables.
  • Casterton Golf Club, next to the school: 9 holes played twice (par 70), with white, yellow and red tees at the distances on the club's scorecard; the nine-hole Par 3, the driving range, and footgolf and rugbygolf on the same holes («Footgolf and more» button).
  • Inside the school: the ground floor of the main building with reception, library, classrooms (sums on the board in the maths room), lab, assembly hall and dining hall, of our own design; outside, its tennis courts.
  • Cars and aircraft: cars in the car parks of the school, the golf club and Kirkby Lonsdale, and helicopters and flying cars on three helipads (school, golf club and Kirkby Lonsdale).
  • Kirkby Lonsdale, with St Mary's church, Ruskin's View over the Lune and the Devil's Bridge, the medieval bridge.
  • The meadows, divided by dry-stone walls and hedges you can't pass through, with gates that open when you arrive, stone farms and sheep.
  • Horses, routes and places: the riding centre's jumping arena by the stables, five real routes along the bridleways (to the Devil's Bridge, Kirkby Lonsdale and Ruskin's View, Holy Trinity and Casterton Grange, Barbon and the stone circle), the bridges you can cross and the places with signs.

What comes from real data

  • Terrain: the Environment Agency LIDAR, with 1 m detail (here, every 4 m); around it, the 2 m one; and the region, the 30 m Copernicus model.
  • Houses: ${0} buildings with their footprint from OpenStreetMap and the Ordnance Survey; the LIDAR measures the height of each.
  • Trees: ${1} treetops found in the LIDAR, with their position and size.
  • Walls and hedges: those in OpenStreetMap, plus the long thin lines, half a metre to two and a half metres high, that show up in the LIDAR.
  • Ground: there is no open aerial photo of Casterton, so it is painted: the colour from the Sentinel-2 satellite (10 m); the relief of every treetop, hedge, wall and roof, with its shadow, from the LIDAR; paths, water, sports fields and gardens from OpenStreetMap.
  • Water: the River Lune in stretches, each with its own level, and the ponds.

What is approximate

  • Walls and roofs follow the local style (grey stone, white sash windows and slate), not each house's own.
  • The species of each tree.
  • A wall and a hedge are told apart by their height in the LIDAR: a few may be swapped.
